citation.title: Interval Estimation of Population Means under Unknown but Bounded Probabilities of Sample Selection

standing_assumptions:
Finite-population (design-based) sampling setting; every probability is over the sampling design. Transcribed from the page images of main.pdf (Biometrika 100(1), 235-240; printed page = PDF page + 234). The proof of Proposition 1 is in the Appendix (pp. 239-240, PDF pp. 5-6); the proofs of Lemma 1 and of Propositions 2 and 3 are in the official supplement (staged/supplements/Bka-12-198_supplement.pdf, 2 pp., cited below as 'Supplement p. 1/2').

(S1) Population, sample, ordering, estimand [Section 2, p. 235 (PDF p. 1)]: 'Consider a population $U$ indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, N$, with associated responses $y_i \in \mathbb{R}$. Let $I_i = 1$ if unit $i$ is sampled from the population; otherwise, let $I_i = 0$. Under a given sampling design, the probability of $i$ being selected is $\pi_i$, so that $\mathrm{pr}(I_i = 1) = \pi_i$. Without loss of generality, assume an index ordering such that the first $n$ units are the sampled units and the remaining $N - n$ are the unsampled units; that is, $I_i = 1$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$ and $I_i = 0$ for $i = n+1, \ldots, N$, so that the set of sampled units is $S = \{1, \ldots, n\}$. Further, let the units in $S$ be ordered so that $y_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant y_n$. The goal is to estimate the population mean, $\mu = \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i/N$.'

(S2) Horvitz-Thompson and Hajek estimators [Section 2, pp. 235-236 (PDF pp. 1-2)]: 'When the probabilities of sample selection are known, and if $\pi_i > 0$ for all $i$, then the Horvitz-Thompson estimator of $\mu$, $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (I_i y_i)/(N\pi_i)$, is unbiased. Similarly, we can define a random variable that has expectation 1: $\hat 1_{\mathrm{HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} I_i/(N\pi_i)$. The Hajek (1971) ratio estimator of $\mu$ is then $\hat\mu = \dfrac{\hat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}}}{\hat 1_{\mathrm{HT}}} = \dfrac{\sum_{i\in S}\pi_i^{-1}y_i}{\sum_{i\in S}\pi_i^{-1}} = \dfrac{w'y}{w'1_n}$, (1) where $w = (w_1, \ldots, w_n) = (\pi_1^{-1}, \ldots, \pi_n^{-1})$, $y = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)$, and $1_n$ is an $n$-vector of ones.'

(S3) Bounded probabilities and the two optimisation problems [Section 3.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 2)]: 'Suppose that we no longer have exact knowledge of the sampling design, instead knowing only that $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$ for all $i$. While consistent point estimation is no longer possible without further assumptions, it is possible to obtain an interval estimate for $\mu$. In fact, sharp bounds for the Hajek estimator (1) exist, in the sense that the set of all possible values of $\hat\mu$ is precisely the interval $[\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}, \hat\mu^{\mathrm H}]$. If $\pi_i \in [\alpha, \beta]$, an upper bound on $\hat\mu$ is $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H} = \max_w\left\{\dfrac{w'y}{w'1_n} : 1/\beta \leqslant w_1, \ldots, w_n \leqslant 1/\alpha\right\}$. (2) Likewise, a lower bound is $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = \min_w\left\{\dfrac{w'y}{w'1_n} : 1/\beta \leqslant w_1, \ldots, w_n \leqslant 1/\alpha\right\}$. (3)' The ratio $\gamma$ is introduced in Proposition 1 (p. 236): 'Let $\gamma = \beta/\alpha \geqslant 1$ be the relative magnitude of $\beta$ compared to $\alpha$.'

(S4) Brewer scaling [Section 3.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 3)]: 'The proposed interval estimator yields asymptotically sharp bounds on $\mu$ itself under the scaling proposed by Brewer (1979) and articulated in Assumption 1.' 'Assumption 1. The sequences of finite populations $\{U_h\}_{h=1}^{\infty}$ and samples $\{S_h\}_{h=1}^{\infty}$ grow as follows. For each $h \geqslant 1$, $U_h = \{U_{h-1}, U\} = \{U, \ldots, U\}$, i.e., $U_h$ consists of $h$ replicates of the original population $U$, so that $|U_h| = hN$. For each $h$, a sample $s_h$ is drawn from $U$ according to the original sampling design, independent of $s_1, \ldots, s_{h-1}$; hence $S_h = \{S_{h-1}, s_h\} = \{s_1, \ldots, s_h\}$. The estimators $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ follow equations (2) and (3), respectively, but applied to the population $U_h$ and the sample $S_h$.'

(S5) Outcome classes, class totals, the limiting optimisation problems [Section 3.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 3)]: 'Let $Y$ be the ordered set of distinct outcomes in $U$, so that $y_{(1)} < \cdots < y_{(|Y|)}$, with equivalence classes $\Upsilon_j \equiv \{i = 1, \ldots, N : y_i = y_{(j)}\}$. In the limit of the Brewer scaling, the probabilities $\pi_i$ can be identified up to units with identical outcomes: as $h \to \infty$, $(\sum_{\{i=1,\ldots,Nh : y_i = y_{(j)}\}} I_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{Nh} I_i) \to \Pi_j/(\sum_{k=1}^{|Y|}\Pi_k)$ where $\Pi_j = \sum_{i\in\Upsilon_j}\pi_i$. Since $\pi_i \geqslant \alpha > 0$ for all $i$, $Y$ is identified in the limit. If $W_j \equiv |\Upsilon_j|/\Pi_j$ is known for all $j = 1, \ldots, |Y|$, then $\mu$ is identified: $\mu = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j} = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j \frac{\Pi_j}{\sum_{k=1}^{|Y|}\Pi_k} y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\frac{\Pi_j}{\sum_{k=1}^{|Y|}\Pi_k}}$. However, $W_j$ is actually only identified up to the interval $\beta^{-1} \leqslant W_j \leqslant \alpha^{-1}$; so in the limit, $\mu$ can be identified up to the interval bounded by $\mu_+ = \max_W\left\{\dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j} : 1/\beta \leqslant W_1, \ldots, W_{|Y|} \leqslant 1/\alpha\right\}$ (6) and $\mu_- = \min_W\left\{\dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j} : 1/\beta \leqslant W_1, \ldots, W_{|Y|} \leqslant 1/\alpha\right\}$. (7)'

(S6) Assumption 2 [Section 3.2, p. 238 (PDF p. 4)], preceded by: 'By Proposition 2, if $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h \to \mu_+$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h \to \mu_-$ as $h \to \infty$, then $[\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h, \hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h]$ is asymptotically sharp. A mild technical condition on $k_+$ and $k_-$ is necessary to guarantee convergence.' 'Assumption 2. For any $k \geqslant 0$, $y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$, $\quad y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$.'

(S7) Reading conventions; these are not printed. They are the ones the validators fixed (validated.json, natural_reading fields) and every target uses them. (a) $n \geqslant 1$, $|Y| \geqslant 1$, and an empty sum is $0$. (b) A rule of the form 'the smallest nonnegative integer $k$ that satisfies [...] $y_{k+1}$' ranges over the integers $0 \leqslant k \leqslant n-1$, the only $k$ for which $y_{k+1}$ is defined; likewise $0 \leqslant k \leqslant |Y|-1$ for a rule in $y_{(k+1)}$ and for Assumption 2. (c) The objective of (2)-(3) is unchanged when $w$ is multiplied by a positive constant, so with $u = \beta w$ the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n$ becomes $[1, \gamma]^n$. For $0 \leqslant k \leqslant n$ write $F^{\mathrm H}_k = \{\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i\}/\{k + \gamma(n-k)\}$ and $F^{\mathrm L}_k = \{\gamma\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i\}/\{\gamma k + (n-k)\}$: these are the values of $w'y/(w'1_n)$ at the threshold vectors $w^{k}$ (first $k$ entries $1/\beta$, last $n-k$ entries $1/\alpha$; Appendix, p. 239) and (first $k$ entries $1/\alpha$, last $n-k$ entries $1/\beta$), respectively. The same holds with class totals: for $0 \leqslant k \leqslant |Y|$, $G^{+}_k = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$ and $G^{-}_k = \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$ are the values of the objective of (6)-(7) at the threshold vectors (first $k$ entries $1/\beta$, rest $1/\alpha$) and (first $k$ entries $1/\alpha$, rest $1/\beta$). (d) $\Pi_j > 0$ for every $j$, because each class $\Upsilon_j$ is nonempty and $\pi_i \geqslant \alpha > 0$; hence every denominator in (6), (7) and in $G^{\pm}_k$ is positive. (e) In Section 3.2 the estimators $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$, $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ are (2) and (3) computed from the pooled sample $S_h$ (all sampled units of the $h$ replicates); they are defined when $S_h$ is nonempty.

(S8) Transcription notes (checked on 420 dpi crops of the page images). (a) In (5) and in the dichotomous display the left-hand set is printed with $\pi_N$ (capital $N$), although $\hat\mu$ depends only on $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_n$. (b) Proposition 3 prints $\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$ and $\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ without hats; the sentence two lines above it and Assumption 1 print $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$, $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$. (c) In Proposition 2 the two second sums of the $\mu_-$ display are printed with lower limit $j = k_- - 1$; every other display of the paper has $k+1$ there. (d) The rule for $k^{\mathrm L}$ (p. 236) and the rule for $k_-$ (p. 238, directly below Table 1) are both printed with $\geqslant$; the rules for $k^{\mathrm H}$ and $k_+$ with $\leqslant$. (e) The supplement sets the superscripts H and L in italic and writes $\leq$, $\geq$; the article sets them upright and writes $\leqslant$, $\geqslant$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Table 1, six entries, corrected: the bounds computed from the counts that the reported sample sizes and percentages imply (44/48, 108/160, 291/579), rounded at the last step
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected entries; Sol's smallest repair, validated.json, P025-N003: 'Use the inferred integer counts and round only final endpoints. Replace gallery L at gamma 2: 84.7 with 84.6; gallery L at gamma 4: 73.4 with 73.3; exchange H at gamma 1.25: 55.9 with 55.8; exchange L at gamma 1.5: 40.3 with 40.2; exchange H at gamma 1.5: 60.3 with 60.2; exchange H at gamma 2.5: 71.7 with 71.6.'] With $L(p, \gamma) = \dfrac{p}{\gamma(1-p)+p}$ and $H(p, \gamma) = \dfrac{\gamma p}{(1-p)+\gamma p}$ (the dichotomous closed form, p. 237) and the sample proportions $p_G = 44/48$, $p_S = 108/160$, $p_E = 291/579$, in percent and to one decimal: shooting gallery, $\gamma = 2$: $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = 84{\cdot}6$ (printed 84·7); shooting gallery, $\gamma = 4$: $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = 73{\cdot}3$ (printed 73·4); needle exchange, $\gamma = 1{\cdot}25$: $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H} = 55{\cdot}8$ (printed 55·9); needle exchange, $\gamma = 1{\cdot}5$: $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = 40{\cdot}2$ (printed 40·3) and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H} = 60{\cdot}2$ (printed 60·3); needle exchange, $\gamma = 2{\cdot}5$: $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H} = 71{\cdot}6$ (printed 71·7). The other 36 entries of Table 1 are unchanged.

[Formal content, each part of the target; from validate/P025-N003/v1/artifact/derivation.md.] (a) [The counts are determined by the reported figures.] The only integer $k$ with $|100k/48 - 91{\cdot}7| \leqslant 0{\cdot}05$ is $k = 44$; the only integer $k$ with $|100k/160 - 67{\cdot}5| \leqslant 0{\cdot}05$ is $k = 108$; the only integer $k$ with $|100k/579 - 50{\cdot}3| \leqslant 0{\cdot}05$ is $k = 291$. (b) [The six exact values.] $100\,L(44/48, 2) = 1100/13 = 84{\cdot}615\ldots$; $100\,L(44/48, 4) = 220/3 = 73{\cdot}333\ldots$; $100\,H(291/579, 5/4) = 48500/869 = 55{\cdot}811\ldots$; $100\,L(291/579, 3/2) = 9700/241 = 40{\cdot}248\ldots$; $100\,H(291/579, 3/2) = 9700/161 = 60{\cdot}248\ldots$; $100\,H(291/579, 5/2) = 48500/677 = 71{\cdot}639\ldots$. Each lies in the half-open interval of width $0{\cdot}1$ centred at the corrected entry ($84{\cdot}55 \leqslant 1100/13 < 84{\cdot}65$, and so on), and each printed entry is $0{\cdot}1$ above the corrected one. (c) [Where the printed entries come from.] With the rounded proportions $917/1000$ and $503/1000$ used as exact inputs, the same six cells are $84{\cdot}672\ldots$, $73{\cdot}418\ldots$, $55{\cdot}851\ldots$, $40{\cdot}288\ldots$, $60{\cdot}287\ldots$, $71{\cdot}672\ldots$, which round to the printed 84·7, 73·4, 55·9, 40·3, 60·3, 71·7; with $917/1000$, $675/1000$, $503/1000$ as inputs all 42 printed entries are reproduced. (d) [The remaining 36 entries.] For every other cell of Table 1, $100\,L$ or $100\,H$ at the count proportion and at the row's $\gamma \in \{1, 5/4, 3/2, 2, 5/2, 3, 4\}$ rounds to the printed entry. (e) [No comparison on the grid changes.] With the count proportions, as with the printed entries, the gallery and exchange intervals are disjoint for $\gamma \leqslant 3$ on the grid and overlap at $\gamma = 4$ ($L(44/48, 3) = 11/14 > H(291/579, 3) = 291/387$; $L(44/48, 4) = 11/15 < H(291/579, 4) = 97/121$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Dichotomous closed form, p. 237 (PDF p. 3)] 'A simple closed-form solution for the bounds in (5) is available when $y$ is dichotomous. Assuming $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$, define $p = \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i/n$. Then, by applying Lemma 1, $\{\hat\mu : \alpha \leqslant \pi_1, \ldots, \pi_N \leqslant \beta,\ y_i \in \{0,1\}\} = \left[\dfrac{p}{\gamma(1-p)+p},\ \dfrac{\gamma p}{(1-p)+\gamma p}\right]$.' [Section 4, p. 238 (PDF p. 4)] 'For (i), a sample of 48 needles was collected from a shooting gallery and tested; of these, 91·7% of needles tested positive for HIV. [...] 160 street needles and 579 exchange needles were tested: 67·5% and 50·3% tested positive, respectively.' [Table 1, p. 238 (PDF p. 4): 'Estimated bounds for prevalence rates (%) of HIV proviral DNA in syringes collected as part of the New Haven syringe tracking and testing programme'; columns $\gamma$ | $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}$ | $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}$] Shooting gallery, $n = 48$: 1 | 91·7 | 91·7; 1·25 | 89·8 | 93·2; 1·5 | 88·0 | 94·3; 2 | 84·7 | 95·7; 2·5 | 81·5 | 96·5; 3 | 78·6 | 97·1; 4 | 73·4 | 97·8. Street, $n = 160$: 1 | 67·5 | 67·5; 1·25 | 62·4 | 72·2; 1·5 | 58·1 | 75·7; 2 | 50·9 | 80·6; 2·5 | 45·4 | 83·9; 3 | 40·9 | 86·2; 4 | 34·2 | 89·3. Needle exchange, $n = 579$: 1 | 50·3 | 50·3; 1·25 | 44·7 | 55·9; 1·5 | 40·3 | 60·3; 2 | 33·6 | 66·9; 2·5 | 28·8 | 71·7; 3 | 25·2 | 75·2; 4 | 20·2 | 80·2. Rounding is to the nearest tenth of a percentage point; none of the 42 exact values is a rounding tie.
canonical_claim.note: P025-N003 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json): six table entries are 0.1 percentage point above the correctly rounded bounds for the samples described, because the rounded percentages were used as inputs. It is a numerical error whose correction changes printed values of a formula, so it is listed at priority 3 on the author's instruction; every part is exact rational arithmetic. The counts are inferred from the article's sample sizes and percentages, not recovered from Kaplan (1991); part (a) is the inference. Repair cost recorded by Sol: none. All 42 cells, the six differences and the uniqueness of the counts were re-verified here in rational arithmetic.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.1, paragraph after (5): 'The bounds do not depend on the actual values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$, only on the ratio $\gamma$. When $\gamma = 1$, we have equal-probability sample selection.'
canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 236 (PDF p. 2)] 'The bounds do not depend on the actual values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$, only on the ratio $\gamma$. When $\gamma = 1$, we have equal-probability sample selection. Higher values of $\gamma$ represent a greater potential for variation in the probabilities of sample selection; for instance, $\gamma = 5$ indicates that some units may be up to five times more likely to be sampled than others.'

[Formal content.] Let $n \geqslant 1$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$. (a) [Dependence on $\gamma$ only.] If $0 < \alpha \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$ and $0 < \alpha' \leqslant \beta' \leqslant 1$ with $\beta/\alpha = \beta'/\alpha' = \gamma$, then $\{w'y/(w'1_n) : w \in [1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n\} = \{w'y/(w'1_n) : w \in [1/\beta', 1/\alpha']^n\} = \{u'y/(u'1_n) : u \in [1, \gamma]^n\}$; in particular the values of (2) and (3) are the same for $(\alpha, \beta)$ and $(\alpha', \beta')$. (b) [Equal probabilities.] If $\gamma = 1$, the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n$ is the single point $(1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha)$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = \hat\mu^{\mathrm H} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i/n$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: (S1)-(S3) of the standing assumptions: the sample $y_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant y_n$, the Hajek estimator (1) $\hat\mu = w'y/(w'1_n)$ with $w_i = \pi_i^{-1}$, the bounds $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$, the problems (2) and (3) over the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n$, and $\gamma = \beta/\alpha \geqslant 1$ [all p. 235-236 (PDF pp. 1-2)].
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P025-H2, an exact finite-sample statement; both fresh readers checked it and it held up (the objective is invariant to rescaling w; at gamma = 1 the box is a point). The last sentence of the quotation is interpretive and is not part of the formal content. The closed forms (4) and (5) depend on (alpha, beta) only through gamma as well; that is part of P025-T3.

canonical_claim.location: p. 237 (PDF p. 3); proof in the Supplement, p. 1
canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 237 (PDF p. 3)] 'A property of the optimal weights $w^{\mathrm H}$ and $w^{\mathrm L}$ is that observations with identical outcomes share the same weight. The following lemma formalizes this assertion and is important for establishing the asymptotic properties of $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}$. LEMMA 1. If $y_k = y_{k+1}$, then $w^{\mathrm H}_k = w^{\mathrm H}_{k+1}$ and $w^{\mathrm L}_k = w^{\mathrm L}_{k+1}$.'

[Formal content.] Let $n \geqslant 2$, $y_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant y_n$, $0 < \alpha \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$, $\gamma = \beta/\alpha$; let $w^{\mathrm H}$ be the vector of Proposition 1 with cut point $k^{\mathrm H}$ (smallest $k \in \{0, \ldots, n-1\}$ with $F^{\mathrm H}_k \leqslant y_{k+1}$), and let $w^{\mathrm L}$ be the vector of Proposition 1 with the corrected cut point $k^{\mathrm L}$ (smallest $k \in \{0, \ldots, n-1\}$ with $F^{\mathrm L}_k \leqslant y_{k+1}$; P025-T3). For every $k \in \{1, \ldots, n-1\}$ with $y_k = y_{k+1}$: $w^{\mathrm H}_k = w^{\mathrm H}_{k+1}$ and $w^{\mathrm L}_k = w^{\mathrm L}_{k+1}$. Equivalently, when $\gamma > 1$: $k^{\mathrm H} \neq k$ and $k^{\mathrm L} \neq k$ whenever $y_k = y_{k+1}$ (no cut point separates two tied observations). [Steps of the Supplement's proof for $w^{\mathrm H}$, p. 1.] (i) If $y_1 = \cdots = y_n$ then $k^{\mathrm H} = 0$ and $w^{\mathrm H} = (1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha)$. (ii) Otherwise $k^{\mathrm H} > 0$, since $F^{\mathrm H}_0 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i/n > y_1$. (iii) If $1 \leqslant k \leqslant k^{\mathrm H}$ and $y_k = y_{k+1}$, then $F^{\mathrm H}_{k-1} > y_k$ and $F^{\mathrm H}_k = \dfrac{(1-\gamma)y_k + \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k}^{n} y_i}{k + \gamma(n-k)} > \dfrac{(1-\gamma)y_k + (k - 1 + \gamma(n-k+1))y_k}{k + \gamma(n-k)} = y_k = y_{k+1}$, so $k + 1 \leqslant k^{\mathrm H}$. (iv) [Lower half, 'in the same manner'.] If $1 \leqslant k \leqslant k^{\mathrm L}$ and $y_k = y_{k+1}$, then $F^{\mathrm L}_{k-1} > y_k$ and $F^{\mathrm L}_k - y_k = \dfrac{\{\gamma(k-1) + (n-k+1)\}(F^{\mathrm L}_{k-1} - y_k)}{\gamma k + (n-k)} > 0$, so $F^{\mathrm L}_k > y_{k+1}$ and $k + 1 \leqslant k^{\mathrm L}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: (S1)-(S3) of the standing assumptions: the sample $y_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant y_n$, the Hajek estimator (1) $\hat\mu = w'y/(w'1_n)$ with $w_i = \pi_i^{-1}$, the bounds $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$, the problems (2) and (3) over the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n$, and $\gamma = \beta/\alpha \geqslant 1$ [all p. 235-236 (PDF pp. 1-2)]. [Proposition 1, p. 236] $w^{\mathrm H}$, $k^{\mathrm H}$ as printed (P025-T7); $w^{\mathrm L}$, $k^{\mathrm L}$ as corrected (P025-T3). Conventions (S7): empty sums are $0$; cut-point rules range over the $k$ for which the next outcome is defined; $F^{\mathrm H}_k$, $F^{\mathrm L}_k$, $G^{+}_k$, $G^{-}_k$ as in (S7c).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P025-H3, first part; an exact finite-sample statement. Both fresh readers followed the Supplement's proof and it held up, including the case of all outcomes equal; numerically no tied pair straddles the cut for k^H or for the corrected k^L. The lemma refers to w^L, whose cut point is misprinted in Proposition 1 (finding P025-E001): with the printed rule k^L = 0 always, all entries of w^L are equal and the w^L half is true but empty; the target states it for the corrected k^L, which is the content the paper intends and uses in Section 3.2. Step (iii) is transcribed from the Supplement's display; step (iv) is the mirror image, which the Supplement leaves to the reader ('The result for w^L can also be established in the same manner').

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.1, closed form of the bounds for a dichotomous outcome (unnumbered display after Lemma 1)
canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 237 (PDF p. 3)] 'A simple closed-form solution for the bounds in (5) is available when $y$ is dichotomous. Assuming $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$, define $p = \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i/n$. Then, by applying Lemma 1, $\{\hat\mu : \alpha \leqslant \pi_1, \ldots, \pi_N \leqslant \beta,\ y_i \in \{0,1\}\} = \left[\dfrac{p}{\gamma(1-p)+p},\ \dfrac{\gamma p}{(1-p)+\gamma p}\right]$.'

[Formal content.] Let $n \geqslant 1$, $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$, $p = \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i/n$, $0 < \alpha \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$ and $\gamma = \beta/\alpha$. Then $\{w'y/(w'1_n) : w \in [1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n\} = \left[\dfrac{p}{\gamma(1-p)+p},\ \dfrac{\gamma p}{(1-p)+\gamma p}\right]$; in particular $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = \dfrac{p}{\gamma(1-p)+p}$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H} = \dfrac{\gamma p}{(1-p)+\gamma p}$. The cases $p = 0$ and $p = 1$ (both endpoints equal $p$) and $\gamma = 1$ (both endpoints equal $p$) are included. [Derivation the validators and readers used.] With $A$ the sum of the weights $\beta w_i$ on the $np$ units with $y_i = 1$ and $C$ the sum on the $n(1-p)$ units with $y_i = 0$, the estimator is $A/(A + C)$ with $np \leqslant A \leqslant \gamma np$ and $n(1-p) \leqslant C \leqslant \gamma n(1-p)$; it is nondecreasing in $A$ and nonincreasing in $C$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: (S1)-(S3) of the standing assumptions: the sample $y_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant y_n$, the Hajek estimator (1) $\hat\mu = w'y/(w'1_n)$ with $w_i = \pi_i^{-1}$, the bounds $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$, the problems (2) and (3) over the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n$, and $\gamma = \beta/\alpha \geqslant 1$ [all p. 235-236 (PDF pp. 1-2)]. [Equation (5), p. 236] as in P025-T7 (the display specialises the set on its left side). [Lemma 1, p. 237] as in P025-T19.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P025-H3, second part; an exact finite-sample statement that underlies every entry of Table 1. It held up for both fresh readers, including p = 0, p = 1 and gamma = 1. It agrees with the corrected Proposition 1 (P025-T3) and disagrees with the printed rule for k^L (at p = 1/2, gamma = 2 it gives 1/3; the printed rule gives 1/2; P025-T1). The left side is printed with pi_N (S8a).

canonical_claim.location: p. 238 (PDF p. 4); proof in the Supplement, p. 2
canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 238 (PDF p. 4)] 'By Proposition 2, if $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h \to \mu_+$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h \to \mu_-$ as $h \to \infty$, then $[\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h, \hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h]$ is asymptotically sharp. A mild technical condition on $k_+$ and $k_-$ is necessary to guarantee convergence.' 'Assumption 2. For any $k \geqslant 0$, $y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$, $\quad y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$.' 'PROPOSITION 3. If Assumptions 1 and 2 hold, then as $h \to \infty$, $\mu^{\mathrm H}_h \to \mu_+$ and $\mu^{\mathrm L}_h \to \mu_-$ almost everywhere.'

[Reading under which it is stated, fixed by the validator.] $\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$ and $\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ are the estimators $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ of Assumption 1 (the hats are missing in print; no unhatted $\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$, $\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ is defined); Assumption 2 is required for the integers $0 \leqslant k < |Y|$, the only $k$ for which $y_{(k+1)}$ is defined; $\mu_+$ and $\mu_-$ are (6) and (7); 'almost everywhere' is with respect to the joint law of the independent replicate samples $s_1, s_2, \ldots$ of Assumption 1. Statement: if the population and design satisfy (S1)-(S3), Assumption 1 and Assumption 2, then $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h \to \mu_+$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h \to \mu_-$ as $h \to \infty$, almost surely.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: (S1)-(S3) of the standing assumptions: the sample $y_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant y_n$, the Hajek estimator (1) $\hat\mu = w'y/(w'1_n)$ with $w_i = \pi_i^{-1}$, the bounds $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$, the problems (2) and (3) over the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n$, and $\gamma = \beta/\alpha \geqslant 1$ [all p. 235-236 (PDF pp. 1-2)]. (S4)-(S5) of the standing assumptions: $Y$, $y_{(1)} < \cdots < y_{(|Y|)}$, $\Upsilon_j$, $\Pi_j = \sum_{i\in\Upsilon_j}\pi_i$, $W_j \equiv |\Upsilon_j|/\Pi_j$, the identity $\mu = \sum_j W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}/\sum_j W_j\Pi_j$, and the problems (6) and (7) over the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^{|Y|}$ [all p. 237 (PDF p. 3)]. [Assumption 1, p. 237] as in (S4). [Lemma 1, p. 237] as in P025-T19. [Proposition 2, pp. 237-238] $k_+$, $W_+$ as printed (P025-T8); $k_-$, $W_-$ as corrected (P025-T4). Conventions (S7): empty sums are $0$; cut-point rules range over the $k$ for which the next outcome is defined; $F^{\mathrm H}_k$, $F^{\mathrm L}_k$, $G^{+}_k$, $G^{-}_k$ as in (S7c).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Supplement, proof of Proposition 3, p. 2] 'Fix a sample realization $\omega \in \Omega = \{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ so that $I_1(\omega), I_2(\omega), \ldots$ is a deterministic binary sequence. We drop the explicit dependence on $\omega$ for brevity. For a $W \in [\beta^{-1}, \alpha^{-1}]^{|Y|}$, define $\mu_h(W) \equiv \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j y_{(j)}\sum_{\{i=1,\ldots,Nh : y_i = y_{(j)}\}} I_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\sum_{\{i=1,\ldots,Nh : y_i = y_{(j)}\}} I_i}$. By Lemma 1, the maximization problem (2) yields the same optimum as maximizing $\mu_h(W)$. Denote $P_{h,j} \equiv h^{-1}\sum_{\{i=1,\ldots,Nh : y_i = y_{(j)}\}} I_i$. By the strong law of large numbers $P_{h,j} \to \Pi_j$ as $h \to \infty$. Therefore $\hat\mu^{H}_h = \max_{W\in[\beta^{-1},\alpha^{-1}]^{|Y|}} \mu_h(W)$, (B3) $\ \mu_h(W) = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j P_{h,j} y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j P_{h,j}} \to \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j}$. (B4) For a sufficiently large $h$, $P_{h,j}$ will be close enough to $\Pi_j$ for the optimal solution to (B3) to be identical to the optimal solution to (6), $W_+$, as characterized in Proposition 2. Formally, Assumption 2 implies that there exists $h_0$ such that, for all $h \geq h_0$, $\dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k_+-1} P_{h,j}y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k_+}^{|Y|} P_{h,j}y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k_+-1} P_{h,j} + \gamma\sum_{j=k_+}^{|Y|} P_{h,j}} > y_{(k_+)}$, $\dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k_+} P_{h,j}y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k_++1}^{|Y|} P_{h,j}y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k_+} P_{h,j} + \gamma\sum_{j=k_++1}^{|Y|} P_{h,j}} < y_{(k_++1)}$ hence $\hat\mu^{H}_h = \mu_h(W_+)$ for all $h \geq h_0$ in view of the characterization of $k_+$ in Proposition 2. Then (B4) implies that $\hat\mu^{H}_h \to \mu_+$ along each sample path $\omega$. The convergence of $\hat\mu^{L}_h$ can be established in the same manner.' [Exact statements for each fixed $h$ in that proof.] Write $C_{h,j}$ for the number of units of $S_h$ with outcome $y_{(j)}$, $P_{h,j} = C_{h,j}/h$, and $f(W, p) = \sum_j W_j p_j y_{(j)}/\sum_j W_j p_j$. (F1) [(B3).] If $S_h$ is nonempty, $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h = \max_{W \in [1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^{|Y|}} f(W, P_h)$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h = \min_{W \in [1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^{|Y|}} f(W, P_h)$. (F2) [(B4), the identity.] $\mu_h(W) = f(W, P_h)$ for every $W$ and every $h$ with $S_h$ nonempty. (F3) [Cut-point stabilisation.] Let $p \in (0, \infty)^{|Y|}$ and let $k_+(p)$ be the smallest $k \in \{0, \ldots, |Y|-1\}$ with $\dfrac{\sum_{j \leqslant k} p_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j > k} p_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j \leqslant k} p_j + \gamma\sum_{j > k} p_j} \leqslant y_{(k+1)}$. If, for some $k^* \geqslant 1$, the two displayed strict inequalities of the proof hold for $p$ with $k_+$ replaced by $k^*$ (the expression at $k^* - 1$ exceeds $y_{(k^*)}$ and the expression at $k^*$ is below $y_{(k^*+1)}$), then $k_+(p) = k^*$ and $\max_W f(W, p)$ is attained at the threshold vector with cut $k^*$ (by P025-T4 applied to the class totals $p$; the set of $k$ that satisfy the test is closed upwards, because $G^{+}_k \leqslant y_{(k+1)}$ implies $G^{+}_{k+1} \leqslant y_{(k+1)} < y_{(k+2)}$); when $k^* = 0$ only the second inequality is needed. (F4) [Continuity at a fixed vertex.] For fixed $W$, $p \mapsto f(W, p)$ is continuous at $\Pi$ (all $\Pi_j > 0$). (F5) [Replicate counts.] As in (F4) of P025-T13: $P_{h,j}$ is an average of $h$ independent, identically distributed, bounded counts with mean $\Pi_j$. (Limit steps: the strong law, $P_{h,j} \to \Pi_j$ almost surely; under Assumption 2 the strict inequalities at $k_+ - 1$ and $k_+$ hold for $\Pi$ and therefore for $P_h$ for all large $h$ on that event.) The lower half ('in the same manner') uses the cut point $k_-$ as corrected in P025-T4.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P025-H5, an asymptotic (almost sure) result, so priority 4. It holds as a sufficient-condition statement under the reading given (validator: 'Proposition 3 remains correct as a sufficient-condition statement under the natural notation and domain'); the missing hats, the index range of Assumption 2 and the false necessity sentence are finding P025-E005 (Minor), corrected in P025-T13, whose form (iv) drops Assumption 2 and implies this statement. Two points about the Supplement's proof recorded in the audit as wording, not errors: 'along each sample path' should read 'along almost every sample path' (P025-N007, clarity note), and the sharpness of the limit interval for mu is qualified in P025-T15. The proof uses Assumption 2 only at k = k_+ (and, for the lower half, at k = k_-): the strict inequality at k_+ - 1 holds by the minimality of k_+.
